title: Let Him Kiss Me
subtitle: Song of Songs 1:1–2:7
description: Her voice opens the book: longing for the king, dark and lovely under the sun, and the first charge to the daughters.
paragraphs: The book names itself in one line, “This is Solomon’s Song of Songs,” and then the woman speaks, and she speaks first and most in this book: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is more delightful than wine.” His name is perfume poured out, and the maidens adore him, and she wants to be taken away at a run: “Take me away with you,” “let us hurry! May the king bring me to his chambers.” The chorus answers in delight, praising his love more than wine, and the poem's first movement is set: her longing, his worth, and a court of daughters listening in.

Then she turns to the daughters of Jerusalem about herself: “I am dark, yet lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.” The darkness has a history. “Do not stare because I am dark, for the sun has gazed upon me. My mother’s sons were angry with me; they made me a keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have neglected.” Brothers angry, outdoor labor assigned, her own vineyard untended: the poem gives her a life before it gives her a romance, and it does not explain the brothers or excuse them. She is lovely, sun-marked, and put to work in other people's fields.

Her first question is a shepherd's geography: “Tell me, O one I love, where do you pasture your sheep? Where do you rest them at midday? Why should I be like a veiled woman beside the flocks of your companions?” The answer sends her along the flock's tracks to the shepherds' tents, and then his voice arrives with its startling comparison: “I compare you, my darling, to a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots.” In his mouth it is praise, cheeks beautiful with ornaments, a neck with strings of jewels, and the promise of gold ornaments studded with silver follows. The poem's lovers praise each other in the concrete splendors of their world: chariots, jewels, vineyards, and spice.

The exchange warms. “While the king was at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance.” He is to her “a sachet of myrrh resting between my breasts,” “a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi.” He answers: “How beautiful you are, my darling! Oh, how very beautiful! Your eyes are like doves.” She returns it: “How handsome you are, my beloved! Oh, how delightful! The soft grass is our bed.” Their house is the outdoors itself: “The beams of our house are cedars; our rafters are fragrant firs.” Two voices, trading delight line for line, is the poem's basic music, and it is established before anything else happens.

She names herself in flowers: “I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valley.” He lifts the image: “Like a lily among the thorns is my darling among the maidens.” She answers with his shade and fruit: “Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest is my beloved among the young men. I delight to sit in his shade, and his fruit is sweet to my taste.” He has brought her to the house of wine, where “his banner over me is love,” and she is faint with it: “Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am faint with love.” His left hand is under her head and his right arm embraces her, and out of that closeness she speaks the book's refrain for the first time, a charge to the watching daughters: “O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the gazelles and does of the field: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.”

title: The Voice of My Beloved
subtitle: Song of Songs 2:8–3:5
description: He comes leaping over the mountains with the spring call, and the first night search ends in finding and holding.
paragraphs: Her next movement begins with a sound: “Listen! My beloved approaches. Look! Here he comes, leaping across the mountains, bounding over the hills.” He comes like the animals of her refrain: “My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag.” Then the picture tightens to a house and a wall: “Look, he stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, peering through the lattice.” He is near and not yet in, present at the lattice, and she is inside watching him watch for her. The whole poem lives in this nearness and delay.

Through the lattice comes the spring call, his longest speech so far: “Arise, my darling. Come away with me, my beautiful one.” The season is his argument: “For now the winter is past; the rain is over and gone.” “The flowers have appeared in the countryside; the season of singing has come, and the cooing of turtledoves is heard in our land.” “The fig tree ripens its figs; the blossoming vines spread their fragrance. Arise, come away, my darling; come away with me, my beautiful one.” Then his wish turns tender and specific: “O my dove in the clefts of the rock, in the crevices of the cliff, let me see your face, let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet, and your countenance is lovely.” He is asking the hidden dove to come out of the rock.

Between the call and its answer stands a small work order about the vineyards: “Catch for us the foxes,” “the little foxes that ruin the vineyards,” “for our vineyards are in bloom.” Small animals, blooming vines, damage done quietly: the poem's one piece of practical counsel sits among the love songs, and readers have always heard more in it than pest control, though the text says only what it says. Then she speaks the belonging line for the first time: “My beloved is mine and I am his; he pastures his flock among the lilies.” And she sends him off with the day's edge: “Before the day breaks and shadows flee, turn, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of Bether.”

Night reverses the search: “On my bed at night I sought the one I love; I sought him, but did not find him.” She rises and walks the city, streets and squares, seeking. The watchmen find her on their rounds, and her whole speech to them is one question: “Have you seen the one I love?” Just past them, she finds him herself: “I had just passed them when I found the one I love. I held him and would not let go until I had brought him to my mother’s house, to the chamber of the one who conceived me.” Sought, lost, risen, found, held: the poem's first full arc of desire completes in her mother's house, the place of her own beginning.

She closes the movement the way she closed the first, turning from the found beloved to the watching daughters: “O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the gazelles and does of the field: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.” The refrain is identical, word for word, and its placement is the poem's rhythm: longing answered, embrace reached, and then the charge again, as if the finding made the warning more necessary rather than less. Love in this book moves in seasons and searches, and the woman who has held her beloved still tells the daughters to let love wake in its own time.

title: The Wedding Day
subtitle: Song of Songs 3:6–5:1
description: Solomon's procession, the bride praised feature by feature, the locked garden opened, and the friends' blessing.
paragraphs: The poem's center opens with a procession seen from a distance: “Who is this coming up from the wilderness like a column of smoke, scented with myrrh and frankincense from all the spices of the merchant?” It is Solomon's carriage, escorted by sixty of Israel's mightiest men, swords at their sides against the terror of the night. The carriage itself is royal work: timber of Lebanon, posts of silver, base of gold, seat of purple, “Its interior is inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.” And the invitation goes out to the chorus: “Come out, O daughters of Zion, and gaze at King Solomon, wearing the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding,” “the day of his heart’s rejoicing.” The day is named a wedding day, and its joy is the king's own.

Then his voice takes the bride apart feature by feature in praise, and nothing in it is abstract: “How beautiful you are, my darling,” “how very beautiful! Your eyes are like doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down Mount Gilead.” Teeth like newly shorn sheep from the washing, each with its twin and none lost. “Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your mouth is lovely. Your brow behind your veil is like a slice of pomegranate.” Her neck is the tower of David hung with a thousand shields, and the praise descends the way the poem's praise does, in the imagery of flocks and orchards and war: “Your breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle grazing among the lilies.”

The praise reaches its verdict: “You are altogether beautiful, my darling; in you there is no flaw.” Then it becomes an invitation with geography in it: “Come with me from Lebanon, my bride, come with me from Lebanon! Descend from the peak of Amana, from the summits of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of the lions, from the mountains of the leopards.” Predators live in those mountains, and he calls her down from them anyway. What she has done to him is stated as capture: “You have captured my heart, my sister, my bride; you have stolen my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your neck.” The title he uses through this whole movement is that doubled one, sister and bride, family and beloved in one address. “How delightful is your love, my sister, my bride! Your love is much better than wine,” and “Your lips, my bride, drip sweetness like the honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue.”

Then the garden, praised first as closed: “My sister, my bride, you are a garden locked up, a spring enclosed, a fountain sealed.” What grows in the locked garden is the poem's richest inventory: “Your branches are an orchard of pomegranates with the choicest of fruits, with henna and nard,” saffron, calamus, cinnamon, myrrh and aloes, “with all the finest spices.” She is also “a garden spring, a well of fresh water flowing down from Lebanon.” Locked, sealed, enclosed, and flowing: the poem holds the two together, and then she speaks, and what she says opens the gate from inside: “Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind. Breathe on my garden and spread the fragrance of its spices. Let my beloved come into his garden and taste its choicest fruits.” The garden is hers to open, and she opens it.

His answer comes at the head of chapter 5, in the past tense of arrival: “I have come to my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spice. I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.” And over the couple the poem sets a blessing spoken to witnesses, the only outside blessing it gives them: “Eat, O friends, and drink; drink freely, O beloved.” The wedding movement closes there, with the garden entered, the feast tasted, and the friends told to drink freely. What follows in the poem is not the wedding night extended but a separation: a knock in the dark, and a door opened too late.

title: I Opened to My Beloved, but He Had Gone
subtitle: Song of Songs 5:2–6:3
description: A knock in the night, a door opened too late, the watchmen's blows, and her praise of the one she cannot find.
paragraphs: The poem's darkest movement begins in half-sleep: “I sleep, but my heart is awake. A sound! My beloved is knocking.” His voice comes through the door with the night on him: “Open to me, my sister, my darling, my dove, my flawless one. My head is drenched with dew, my hair with the dampness of the night.” Her answer is the small, fatal delay, given in her own words with the verse's dashes standing between her comfort and her excuses: “I have taken off my robe,” “must I put it back on? I have washed my feet,” “must I soil them again?” Robe off, feet washed, bed warm: the poem lets the delay be exactly as small as real delays are.

Then she rises. “My beloved put his hand to the latch; my heart pounded for him.” “I rose up to open for my beloved. My hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with flowing myrrh on the handles of the bolt.” And the door opens onto absence: “I opened for my beloved, but he had turned and gone. My heart sank at his departure. I sought him but did not find him. I called, but he did not answer.” The first night search ended in finding and holding. This one runs the other way, and the city is not kind the second time.

“I encountered the watchmen on their rounds of the city. They beat me and bruised me; they took away my cloak, those guardians of the walls.” The same watchmen who were asked a question in chapter 3 now strike her and strip her cloak, and the poem gives no reason and no rescue. She turns instead to the chorus, with a new charge different from the refrain: “O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you, if you find my beloved, tell him I am sick with love.” The daughters ask the question that unlocks the poem's second great praise: “How is your beloved better than others, O most beautiful among women? How is your beloved better than another, that you charge us so?”

Her answer praises him the way he praised her, feature by feature, in gold and cedar and marble: “My beloved is dazzling and ruddy, outstanding among ten thousand.” “His head is purest gold; his hair is wavy and black as a raven.” “His eyes are like doves beside the streams of water, bathed in milk and mounted like jewels.” His cheeks are beds of spice, his lips lilies dripping myrrh. “His arms are rods of gold set with beryl. His body is polished ivory bedecked with sapphires.” “His legs are pillars of marble set on bases of pure gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, as majestic as the cedars.” And the praise lands where his landed, on a verdict: “His mouth is most sweet; he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.”

The praise has done something: the daughters are converted from questioners to seekers. “Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Which way has he turned? We will seek him with you.” And she knows, suddenly, where he is: “My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to pasture his flock in the gardens and to gather lilies.” The garden he entered in the wedding movement is where the lost beloved is found in her mind, and the movement closes on the belonging line in its second form: “I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me; he pastures his flock among the lilies.” He is gone from her door and present in his garden, both at once, and the poem lets her hold the belonging tighter than the finding.

title: Majestic as Troops with Banners
subtitle: Song of Songs 6:4–7:10
description: His praise renewed above queens and concubines, the Shulammite called back, and the belonging line in its final form.
paragraphs: He answers the separation with praise again, and the praise reaches higher than before: “You are as beautiful, my darling, as Tirzah, as lovely as Jerusalem, as majestic as troops with banners.” A city, a capital, and an army under banners are his comparisons now. Her eyes themselves defeat him: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have overcome me.” Then come verses the reader has met before, and the poem means them to be met again: her hair like the flock of goats streaming down from Gilead, her teeth like sheep from the washing with every twin kept, her brow like the slice of pomegranate. The praise of chapter 4 returns in chapter 6 nearly word for word, because in this poem praise is not information. It is something he does again because she is before him again.

Then the harem is counted only to be set aside: “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number,” “but my dove, my perfect one, is unique, the favorite of the mother who bore her. The maidens see her and call her blessed; the queens and concubines sing her praises.” The queens and concubines themselves join the praise, and the chorus speaks the next line in wonder: “Who is this who shines like the dawn, as fair as the moon, as bright as the sun, as majestic as the stars in procession?” The woman who walked the night streets bruised by watchmen is seen here rising like the dawn, and the poem does not comment on the distance between the two pictures. It lets both stand.

The voice then turns to a walnut grove: “I went down to the walnut grove to see the blossoms of the valley, to see if the vines were budding or the pomegranates were in bloom.” “Before I realized it, my desire had set me among the royal chariots of my people.” Readers have never fully agreed on whose voice this is, and the poem gives no heading to settle it. What follows it is clearer: a call from the watchers for the woman to return and be gazed at: “Come back, come back, O Shulammite! Come back, come back, that we may gaze upon you. Why do you look at the Shulammite, as on the dance of Mahanaim?” Shulammite is the only name the poem gives her, and it comes here, in the mouths of others, alongside a dance.

The praise of the dance descends over her the way his first praise did, feet to head this time: “How beautiful are your sandaled feet, O daughter of the prince! The curves of your thighs are like jewels, the handiwork of a master.” The images run through goblet and wheat and lilies, the twin fawns again, then upward: “Your neck is like a tower made of ivory; your eyes are like the pools of Heshbon by the gate of Bath-rabbim; your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, facing toward Damascus.” “Your head crowns you like Mount Carmel, the hair of your head like purple threads; the king is captured in your tresses.” The king who crowned and processed through the city is now the captive, caught in her hair. “How fair and pleasant you are, O love, with your delights!”

His desire speaks plainly in the palm tree: “Your stature is like a palm tree; your breasts are clusters of fruit.” “I said, ‘I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruit.’” Her mouth is the finest wine, and the verse itself hands her the last word of the exchange, as if the wine flows from his speech into hers: “May it flow smoothly to my beloved, gliding gently over lips and teeth.” Then the belonging line in its third and final form, shorter and changed: “I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me.” First it was possession stated by her, then belonging stated across a separation. Now it is his desire for her that completes the sentence, and the movement ends on it.

title: Let Us Go to the Countryside
subtitle: Song of Songs 7:11–8:7
description: Her dawn invitation to the vineyards, the wish about a brother, and love declared as strong as death.
paragraphs: The last movement opens with her invitation, and it is a working invitation, set early in the morning among the crops: “Come, my beloved, let us go to the countryside; let us spend the night among the wildflowers.” “Let us go early to the vineyards to see if the vine has budded, if the blossom has opened, if the pomegranates are in bloom,” “there I will give you my love.” The vineyard she was once forced to keep for others, while her own went neglected, is now the place she brings him by choice, at dawn, in blossom time. “The mandrakes send forth a fragrance, and at our door is every delicacy, new as well as old, that I have treasured up for you, my beloved.” What she gives is stored and new at once, kept for him at her own door.

Her next words are a wish about the world's watching: “O that you were to me like a brother who nursed at my mother’s breasts! If I found you outdoors, I would kiss you, and no one would despise me.” A brother could be kissed in the street without scorn; a beloved cannot, and she wishes the scorn away. “I would lead you and bring you to the house of my mother who taught me. I would give you spiced wine to drink, the nectar of my pomegranates.” Her mother's house again, as in the first night search: the place of her teaching and her beginning is where she keeps bringing him.

Then the embrace returns, and with it the refrain for the third time: “His left hand is under my head, and his right arm embraces me.” “O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.” It is the poem's closing charge as well as its recurring one. The love that has now been longed for, searched for, wed, lost, praised, and invited to the fields is still not to be forced or hurried by anyone watching. Timing belongs to love itself in this book, from the first charge to the last.

Another voice asks from the edge of the scene: “Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved?” She comes up leaning, the opposite of her solitary night walks. Under the apple tree the words turn to birth: “I roused you under the apple tree; there your mother conceived you; there she travailed and brought you forth.” The poem does not name the speaker of these lines either. It places birth and love under the same tree and moves on to its climax.

The climax is her request and the book's strongest claim: “Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm. For love is as strong as death, its jealousy as unrelenting as Sheol. Its sparks are fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all.” A seal is the mark of ownership and identity, worn over the heart and on the arm, and she asks to be set there permanently. The reason given is not sweetness but strength: love matches death itself in power and gives up nothing. “Mighty waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away. If a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, his offer would be utterly scorned.” Everything the poem has celebrated, wine, wealth, vineyards, kingdoms of queens, is priced in one sentence and found too cheap. Love cannot be bought, drowned, or outlasted, and the book's whole argument gathers into those two verses.

title: My Own Vineyard Is Mine to Give
subtitle: Song of Songs 8:8–14
description: The brothers' plan for the little sister, her answer, the vineyard accounts settled, and her voice last.
paragraphs: The poem's final movement opens with other people's voices, the brothers, planning for a girl not yet grown: “We have a little sister, and her breasts are not yet grown. What shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?” Their plan is architectural: “If she is a wall, we will build a tower of silver upon her. If she is a door, we will enclose her with panels of cedar.” A wall gets silver added; a door gets boarded with cedar. The speakers are usually heard as the woman's own brothers, the same sons of her mother who were angry with her and set her to keep the vineyards in the book's first chapter. The poem gives them this one speech near its end, arranging a future for a sister, and gives her the answer.

Her answer claims her own maturity in their own image: “I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers. So I have become in his eyes like one who brings peace.” She is not the door boarded shut, and not a child being planned for either. She is the wall with towers, standing on her own, and in her beloved's eyes she is the one who brings peace. The book opened with her presented as dark, stared at, worked in other people's vineyards under her brothers' anger. It nears its end with her defining herself in a single sentence and naming what she is to him.

Then come the vineyard accounts, and she keeps the books: “Solomon had a vineyard in Baal-hamon. He leased it to the tenants. For its fruit, each was to bring a thousand shekels of silver.” Solomon's vineyard is a business, farmed out for a fixed royal return. Hers is something else: “But my own vineyard is mine to give; the thousand shekels are for you, O Solomon, and two hundred are for those who tend its fruit.” In the first chapter she said her own vineyard had been neglected while she kept everyone else's. Here, at the end, her vineyard is hers, and hers to give, and the giving is on her terms. The poem's first complaint and its final settlement use the same word.

His voice comes once more, asking only to hear hers: “You who dwell in the gardens, my companions are listening for your voice. Let me hear it!” The book that began with her voice ends with him asking for it, the companions listening in.

And her voice is the last sound in the book: “Come away, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices.” No wedding procession home, no settled household, no summary of the love the poem has praised as stronger than death. She calls him to come away, as he once called her to arise and come away in the springtime of chapter 2, and the poem closes on the call, unanswered on the page. The Song ends the way it lived: her longing spoken aloud, his coming still the next thing.
